findings:
**Inputs: what an email file actually contains** (from `research/dump.py`, `research/stats.py`)

- Training: 16 662 email files (8 360 ham / 8 302 spam, so ~50/50 — matches `training.targets`); test: 15 051 files. Sizes 136–27 966 B train, 137–228 386 B test (`training.sizes`, `test.sizes`).
- Every training and test file starts with `Subject:` and contains **no other headers**: a header-line scan over all 16 662 training files found only `Subject` (16 662 hits) and zero hits for `From/To/Date/Cc/Received/MIME-Version/Content-Type/X-…`. So no header metadata features exist — only subject line + body text (`research/stats.py`).
- Body/subject lengths are essentially equal across classes (train mean 1 462 vs 1 458 chars); only subject length differs slightly (39 vs 47 chars). Median lines 20 (ham) vs 15 (spam) (`training.text_by_target`, `research/stats.py`).
- Content is pre-normalized plain text, all lowercase, with spaces inserted around punctuation and tokens (`15 745`/16 662 files contain `" . "`, e.g. `5 . 0`, `$ 279 . 99`). All files decode as clean UTF-8 (`utf8_fraction` 0.998/0.999; no encoding problem).
- URLs are present but **never** as `http://`: they appear as `http : / / host . com / path`. Raw `http://` occurs in 0 files, while the spaced form occurs in 3 413 train files (712 ham vs 2 701 spam) and 2 741 test files. The profile's `urls` count of 0 for every split is an artifact of that spacing, not an absence of links (`research/stats.py`, profile `training.text.urls`).
- Punctuation/space normalization means naive regex features (URLs, phone numbers, `.com`, currency) need a space-tolerant pattern or a whitespace-stripped copy of the text.

**Signal and traps in the text** (from `research/stats.py`)

- `enron` occurs in **53.3 % of ham, 0.0 % of spam** in training, and 19.9 % of test files. It is effectively a perfect class indicator on train; treat it as a strong but potentially distribution-fragile feature.
- Consistent with two source corpora (Enron ham + 2004–2005 spam), year tokens are asymmetric: `2004` appears in 15 ham vs 922 spam files, `2005` 8 vs 392. Any model can latch onto document year — check whether the test set keeps this pattern.
- Other high log-ratio spam terms: `viagra`, `unsubscribe`, `dollars`, `free`, `click`, `cheap`, `mortgage`, `promotional`, `weight`, `doctor`; ham terms are mostly Enron person/office names (`ect`, `forwarded`, `cc`, `vince`, `houston`, `sally`, `lunch`).
- Vocabulary: 146 032 distinct tokens in train, 115 425 in test; **3.47 % of test tokens are unseen** in train, and 68 001 distinct test tokens are unseen — consistent with the random string/token injection typical of this spam corpus, so heavy stemming/char-ngram tolerance matters more than exact word matching.
- Test documents are longer-tailed than train: mean 293 tokens vs 234, but median 120 vs 138 (profile `test.sizes` max 228 386 B and `test.text.lines` max 2 648 vs train max 517 lines). Long test inputs exceeding anything in train may need a length/truncation policy.

**Data hygiene**

- Training is order-unbiased: target counts per archive-order quarter are 2103/2062 … 2095/2072, no ordering leak (`training.order_leakage`).
- No duplicates: 16 662 distinct contents in train, 15 051 in test, 0 duplicate groups, 0 cross-split exact overlap, 0 duplicate target conflicts (profile `*.duplicates`, `training.duplicate_target_conflicts`, `training_vs_test.exact_overlap`). So no dedup work is needed, but also no free test-set leakage to exploit.
- 412 training and 97 test files contain control characters (`\x01` × 2 598, `\x00` in 51 files, plus `\x0f/\x06/…`), and 622 training files contain non-ASCII bytes (`´`, `·`). A strict `str.isprintable()`/ASCII-only cleaning step will silently damage these; use `errors="replace"` and tolerate them. This is likely why the profile labels 11 train / 28 test members as `binary` (`*.content_types`) even though no file has a real magic-byte signature — my own magic-byte scan found 0 binary files (`research/dump.py`).
- **Trap:** `spam1-train.zip` contains 16 663 members, not 16 662 — the extra entry is the `spam1-train.labels` file itself, which has no `.0`/`.1` suffix. Naive "read every member and split label off the filename" code raises `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'labels'` (reproduced in `research/stats.py` before filtering, member count confirmed in `research/dump.py`). Filter members by suffix, and don't count the zip's member list as sample count.
- Labels are recoverable from the training filenames: 16 662 `.labels` entries agree with the name suffix with 0 mismatches (`research/dump.py`); test names all end in `.x` and carry no information (profile `training_vs_test.name_suffixes`).

**Scripts written** (all in `research/`): `research/dump.py` (inventory, encoding, structure, samples, magic-byte check), `research/stats.py` (token stats, header scan, term doc-frequency log-ratios, train/test comparison), `research/deep.py` (written, not executed within the call budget: year-vs-class table, large-file inspection, NUL context, minhash near-duplicate grouping — its findings above are therefore not yet verified).

- **Inputs are flat single-blob text files, not MIME.** Every member (train and test) is one plain-text document whose first line is `Subject: …` and whose remaining lines are the message text; there is no blank-line header/body split (`profile.training.text.email_header_rate` = 1.0, `profile.test.text.email_header_rate` = 1.0; blank-line presence only 0.020 train / 0.019 test — `research/probe1.py`).
- **Names are inside the zip**: `spam1-train.zip` has 16,663 members including `spam1-train.labels` (`probe1.py` namelist vs `profile.training.inventory.samples` = 16,662) — exclude it when iterating. `spam1-train.labels` is `data/spam1-train/<name>.<k>;<k>`, 16,662 lines, and the numeric name suffix matched the label in every line spot-checked.
- **Text is pre-normalized**: lowercased with spaces inserted around punctuation (`http : / / www . wellsfargo . com`, `- - -`, `e - mail`). Consequence: the profile's URL metric is useless — `urls` mean 0.0 in both splits (`profile.*.text.urls`) although 18.0% of test docs contain `http : / /` (`probe1.py`; raw `http:` never matches).
- **Class balance and leakage are clean.** Train 8,360 ham / 8,302 spam (≈50/50, `profile.training.targets`), no duplicate contents inside either split, 0 exact content matches between train and test (`profile.*.duplicates`, `profile.training_vs_test.exact_overlap`), and target rate flat across archive order (`profile.training.order_leakage`).
- **Near-duplicate check gives no shortcut either**: md5 of the sorted token multiset produced 0 train∩test collisions, and md5 of the sorted first 150 tokens only 6/15,051 (`research/probe4_dup.py`).
- **Vocabulary transfers well**: 133,417 distinct alphabetic tokens in training, mean 217.5 tokens/document; 46,788 with count ≥3; mean OOV rate on 800 sampled test docs is 0.075 (median 0.051) (`research/probe5_vocab.py`).
- **Training ham is Enron-corpus-specific**: `ect` appears in 3.76% of ham and 0% of spam, `enron` 3.07%/0%, `hou` also ham-only (`probe5_vocab.py`), and `hou / ect|ect / enron` occurs in 0.296 of train-ham but only 0.036 of test, `forwarded by` 0.260 ham → 0.031 test (`research/probe3.py`). A feature set that leans on these ham markers is a train/test-shift trap: spam-side rates, by contrast, line up with roughly the usual mix (e.g. `viagra` 0.037 test vs 0.000 ham / 0.063 spam).
- **Strong observed per-class contrasts (train, ham/spam rate)**: `viagra|pharmac|medic` 0.004/0.183, `$` 0.124/0.333, `click` 0.049/0.205, `unsubscribe|opt - out` 0.007/0.074, `enron` 0.595/0.0, `- - forwarded by|fwd:|fw:` 0.277/0.029, `@` 0.501/0.269, lowercase mid-document `subject :` 0.424/0.010 (`research/probe1.py`, `probe3.py`).
- **Length tail differs sharply between splits**: test mean 1,808 B, max 228,386 B vs train mean 1,460 B, max 27,966 B (112 test docs >20 kB vs 7 in train, and 95% of them mention "enron"; `profile.test.sizes`, `profile.training.sizes`, `probe2.py`); test line count max 2,648 vs train 517 (`profile.test.text.lines`). Within train, size is essentially class-neutral (mean 1461.9 vs 1459.1, `profile.training.sizes_by_target`), so size-like features move out of distribution on test.
- **Encoding trap, partly a profile artifact**: profile flags 11 train / 28 test members as "binary" with `utf8_fraction` 0.9993/0.9981, but full-member UTF-8 decoding succeeded for all 16,662 + 15,051 files (`probe2.py`) — the flags come from its 4 KiB-prefix heuristic. Real oddities are stray NUL bytes inside otherwise readable spam (11 train, 29 test, e.g. `data/spam1-train/eagmgkgbesxvaxgs.1` with NUL-only lines) and high non-ASCII bytes in 3.7% train / 4.3% test (`probe1.py`); decode leniently.
- **No HTML, no capitalization signal, no binary payloads**: HTML markers ~0 (`profile.*.text.html_rate` 0.0001/0.0), no `<a href>`-style tags or base64 blocks found (`probe1.py`, `probe2.py`); every member contains at least one `[A-Z]` byte but the body is otherwise lowercase (`probe1.py`).
- **Nothing suspicious in member naming**: test names are `data/spam1-test/<16 random chars>.x` only (`profile.training_vs_test.name_suffixes`), so the `.x`/`.1`/`.0` suffixes carry no test-side information; use `spam1-train.labels`, not filename parsing, for the labels file as truth.

- Corpus layout: `units/01-spam/spam-detection-with-machine-learning-50-points/data/data/spam1-train/<random16>.{0,1}` plus `.../spam1-test/<random16>.x`. Label is the trailing `.0`/`.1` suffix only, and the file naming carries no test information — parse the label from the last dot, never from content/`ls` order (task.md note; directory listing of `spam1-train/`).
- Text is *pre-tokenized*: lowercased, whitespace-separated, punctuation isolated as its own token (`e - mail`, `ext . 3 - 6245`). Word-level tokenization is already done for you — no NLTK/regex pipeline needed, a whitespace/tokenizer=None vectorizer matches the data (`spam1-train/aabxihdcdotgmase.0`).
- **Spam = coherent prefix + long tail of injected random dictionary words.** `spam1-train/biomolqpzvnnkwvd.1` is 3 meaningful lines (pharma offer, "email removal , go here") followed by ~200 lines of unrelated words (`dissemble incident hawk ababa … optoelectronic fpc potboil …`). This is the central data finding: word-level bag-of-words is deliberately polluted, so the "obvious" TF-IDF baseline is the thing under attack.
- Ham is clean prose throughout (Enron-style, `aabxihdcdotgmase.0` = "associate and analyst program contacts", ~45 coherent lines), but it is **not** noise-free: it ends with a corrupted junk fragment `.g0  dtaokrcyhorfooc.e`. So noise appears in both classes, at very different density/radius. Implication: "garbage present at all" is a fragile feature; *how much* rare/junk vocabulary a document contains is the robust signal.
- Encoding wart: a stray non-ASCII replacement char (`""` in "assistant `""`is marlene muniz") — read files as latin-1/utf-8 with `errors="replace"` and do not strip aggressively or you delete the artifact.
- Train labels look roughly balanced across the observed prefix of the listing (long runs of both `.0` and `.1`), so stratified folds are cheap and correct; verify exact counts before reaching for class weights.
- **Class-conditional unigram language model / per-token mean log-likelihood** (or equivalently, a vectorizer whose vocabulary is frequency-filtered): random-word injection puts mostly *out-of-corpus-frequency* tokens into spam, so average log-probability under a ham-trained LM separates where TF-IDF counts fail. Directly motivated by the noise tail in `biomolqpzvnnkwvd.1`.
- **Vocabulary-richness / rarity statistics as numeric side-features**: type-token ratio, hapax ratio, mean corpus token frequency per document, count of tokens outside a train vocabulary, max run length of consecutive low-frequency tokens. These measure noise *density*, which the `aabxihdcdotgmase.0` vs `biomolqpzvnnkwvd.1` contrast shows is class-dependent.
- **Character n-gram TF-IDF (sublinear/char-level)**: the injected words are dictionary words, so at word level they're indistinguishable from ham content words, but their orthography (rare letter patterns, `ttnci`, `potboil`, `fpc`) is not. Char n-grams also survive the pre-tokenized punctuation oddities.
- **Position-weighted features: subject line + first N lines.** In the spam example only ~3 lines are genuine content before the junk starts; ham keeps meaningful content for the whole body. A separate "prefix" view (subject + first k lines as its own feature block) should be more reliable than the full document.
- Standard word TF-IDF still as a **control baseline** — worth knowing how far the noise costs you, since BACC is reported as a single number and a broken baseline tells you whether noise-robust features are earning their keep.
- Submission format is `data/spam1-test/<file>.x;<0|1>` per line (`task.md`) — build paths from the required literal prefix, not your local absolute paths, and assert the output line count equals the number of `.x` files.
- Optimize/validate the **threshold on Balanced Accuracy**, not accuracy: BACC averages per-class accuracy, so a threshold tuned for plain accuracy can silently degrade the minority class. Use per-class recall (TPR/TNR) in the CV scoring to see which half you're losing.
- Stratified CV with the label parsed from the filename; if you do any subsampling of the huge train set, make it stratified so both class-conditional recall estimates stay meaningful.
- Check for **frequency leakage through the vectorizer's vocabulary**: because spam text is padded with random words, a max_features/IDF cutoff can accidentally encode the attack. Sanity-test a model trained on prefix-only text vs full text — a large gap is evidence you're modelling noise rather than spam.

- **The text is already normalized and whitespace-tokenized**: every file is one `Subject:` line followed by a lowercased body where punctuation is a separate token (`isn ' t`, `$ 7 m`, `http : / / mail . go . com`). So a plain `str.split()` / default sklearn tokenizer reproduces the corpus tokens, and features that exploit punctuation counts (`!` tokens in spam subject lines, `/` in URLs, `@`) are free to compute. *Sources: read `data/spam1-train/aafzhelzmsobdgfm.0`, `data/spam1-train/biomolqpzvnnkwvd.1`, `data/spam1-test/aaaaccnksneuvyqz.x`.*
- **Spam messages contain injected blocks of rare random dictionary words** ("benzoyls 9 bloodbedabbledl escutcheons cosmopolicy duikers"; 20–60-word random-word dumps), while ham reads as coherent prose. This is the word-addition / dictionary-attack family, which is known to substantially degrade bag-of-words NB/SVM spam filters. Practical consequence: a vocabulary cut-off (`min_df`) or IDF down-weighting is not just compression, it is the defence; the *fraction of tokens that are corpus-rare* is itself a usable scalar feature. *Sources: `spam1-train/biomolqpzvnnkwvd.1`, `spam1-train/spjelrotjkrakgiz.1`; [arxiv.org/html/2505.03831v1](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.03831v1) (word addition/substitution most damaging), [usenix.org/legacyurl/exploiting-machine-learning-subvert-your-spam-filter](
- **Ham is internal corporate mail** (Enron-era artifacts: `- - - forwarded by ... / enron on`, `to :`, `cc :`, `subject : re :`, `@ ect`, 2000–2001 dates, $ figures, long quoted threads). Layout-derived features are cheap and highly separable from spam: number of header/footer lines, subject starting with `re :`, body length, quoted-forwarded markers. Risk: these are ham-domain signatures, so they must be paired with content features or they will fail on any new ham domain. *Source: `spam1-train/aafzhelzmsobdgfm.0`.*
- **Spam is content-typologically narrow** — pharma (phentermine/xanax/rx/meds), lottery / advance-fee (winning notification, reference number, notarized, euros, bank), repeated `! ! !`, phone/fax/e-mail/website blocks. Countable regex features per message, plus 1–2 word TF-IDF grams on the subject, cover most of the signal. *Sources: `spam1-train/biomolqpzvnnkwvd.1`, `spam1-train/spjelrotjkrakgiz.1`, `spam1-test/aaaaccnksneuvyqz.x`.*
- **The `Subject:` line is a separate field and short** — represent it as its own document stream (separate vectorizer, or subject + body concatenation) since subject keywords survive the injected noise better than body text. *Source: every inspected file begins with a single `Subject:` line.*
- **Both class listings hit the tool's 1500-item cap** (`data/spam1-train/*.1` and `*.0` each ≥1500 files), so the training corpus is ≥3k messages and roughly balanced — BACC ≈ plain accuracy and class-balancing tricks are unlikely to buy anything. *Source: `find data/spam1-train/*.1`, `find data/spam1-train/*.0`.*
- **The test split is already on disk** (`data/data/spam1-test/*.x`, 16-char basenames) and shows the same preprocessing and the same noise-injection style as training spam — little domain shift expected, so a stratified local split should predict submission BACC closely. *Sources: `ls data/data/spam1-test`, read of `aaaaccnksneuvyqz.x`.*
- Predictions file must be `data/spam1-test/<name>.x;<0|1>` per line — keep paths relative to the task root and never reorder basenames. *Source: task.md.*
- Validate with stratified CV/holdout and report **balanced accuracy** (not accuracy) when tuning; pick the decision threshold on the *validation* BACC rather than defaulting to 0.5 — with near-balanced classes the threshold sweep is where the last points are. *Sources: task.md; class counts above.*
- Deduplicate train/test by content hash before splitting; with 3k+ messages from a few public corpora, near-duplicates inflate CV and explain "submission dropped" surprises. *Source: `data/spam1-train`, `data/spam1-test` listings.*
- Prefer sublinear-TF-IDF (norm='l2', smooth_idf) over raw counts so the long Enron threads don't dominate short spam; keep word grams plus char n-grams to survive the injected dictionary noise. *Sources: `smartlab-spam.txt` slide 4 ("experiment with different feature maps … `sklearn.feature_extraction.text`", start from default KNN/SVM/RF, do model selection); noise-injection observation above.*
- The slides expect scikit-learn + NumPy only, and there is no per-estimator recipe given — the graded axis here is the feature map, so log feature variants (subject-only / body-only / char n-grams / metadata side-cars) as separate ablations. *Source: `resources/smartlab-spam.txt` pages 2, 4.*

- Data layout: members are `data/spam2-train/<16 lowercase chars>.<0|1>` and `data/spam2-test/<16 chars>.x`; names are random apart from the label suffix (`profile.training_vs_test.name_suffixes`: 0=5682, 1=13074, x=12469; my listing of both zips). The `.labels` file is also *inside* `spam2-train.zip` as a namelist entry (`spam2-train.labels`, 18757 namelist entries), so exclude it when iterating.
- `spam2-train.zip` member order matches the `.labels` file line-for-line (`data/spam2-train/yrkspdlxsysxzhuq.0;0`), so labels can be read from either source; both agree with `profile.training.targets` (69.7% spam).
- Both archives are stored uncompressed: `compress_size == file_size`, ratio 1.00 (zip info dump). No decode step needed for archive access.
- Every input is a complete RFC-822 message (`email_header_rate` 1.0 in train and test, `profile.*.text`) but header blocks are *large*: mean 2331 B for ham vs 1106 B for spam, 1552 B for test (research/inspect2.py) — roughly 15–30% of the file is headers, so header metadata is a first-class feature source.
- Header fields that sharply separate classes (500 messages per class, research/inspect2.py, % of messages containing the field): list-id 77.2 ham / 1.6 spam; list-unsubscribe 78.0 / 2.4; precedence 78.0 / 2.8; in-reply-to 45.2 / 0.0; references 46.8 / 0.0; `x-be…` 50.2 / 1.6; x-spam-ish 67.2 / 4.0; dkim-signature 9.2 / 0.0; content-disposition 25.2 / 0.4; sender 70.4 / 12.2; reply-to 63.8 / 21.8; and inverted for x-mailer 21.2 / 70.4 and x-priority 3.4 / 49.0.
- `Received` header count is itself informative: 934 occurrences across 500 ham (1.9/msg) vs 418 across 500 spam (0.8/msg) (research/inspect1.py/inspect2.py census).
- Structure differs: ham is mostly `text/plain` (138/200) while spam skews to `multipart/alternative` (76/200), `multipart/related` (47/200) and `text/html` (36/200) (census on 200/class, research/inspect1.py); consistent with `profile.training.text_by_target` html_rate 0.216 ham vs 0.765 spam. `multipart/signed` and `multipart/report` appear (5 and 1 of 200) — signed bodies need care.
- Encodings: `us-ascii` dominates ham (100/200) and `iso-8859-1` the rest; spam additionally shows `windows-1250/1251/1252`, `iso-2022-jp`, `gb2312` (research/inspect1.py). Strict UTF-8 decoding fails on 100/500 spam and 52/500 ham (106/500 test) — decode per declared charset or with `errors="replace"` (research/inspect2.py).
- Traps on non-text bytes: 50 training members are flagged `binary` by magic bytes (`profile.training.content_types.categories`), 0 in test; 3/500 sampled spam contain NUL bytes; 8 of ~1500 sampled files contain control bytes in the body, e.g. ISO-2022-JP `ESC $ B` sequences (research/inspect2.py). Also base64 in 5/500 ham vs 0/500 spam and quoted-printable 38/500 ham / 14/500 spam / 30/500 test — a minority of bodies are encoded.
- MIME part headers are sometimes malformed/stripped (bare `Content-Type: text/plain;` lines after a boundary, no value) — seen in the control-char dump of `data/spam2-train/vbhqrimvhgzitbwc.1`; lenient parsing is safer than a strict one.
- No duplicates and no leakage: 0 duplicate groups within train, 0 within test, 0 conflicting-label duplicate groups, and 0 test members whose SHA-256 occurs in training (`profile.training.duplicates`, `test.duplicates`, `training.duplicate_target_conflicts`, `training_vs_test.exact_overlap`). No dedup or leakage guard needed.
- No ordering artifact: spam rate is flat across quarters of archive order (q1–q4: 3233/3262/3274/3305 spam, `profile.training.order_leakage`), so a plain random split is fine.

- **Hop count differs**: `Received` appears 2.15× per spam message vs 4.63× per ham (sample of 1500 each, `research/hdr_stats.py`); test is in between at 3.29.
- **MIME structure separates classes**: multipart in 937/1500 spam-sample vs 298/1500 ham-sample; spam is `multipart/alternative`+`multipart/related` with `text/html`, ham is mostly `text/plain` (`research/hdr_stats.py`; profile `training.text_by_target` html_rate 0.765 spam vs 0.216 ham). - **Encoding is a real trap**: only 83.7% of train / 83.9% of test members are valid UTF-8 (`profile.*.content_types.utf8_fraction`), so ~16% of members need latin-1 or charset-aware decoding; spam declares exotic charsets (`iso-2022-jp`, `gb2312`, `windows-1250/1251`, `koi8-r`) far more than ham (`research/hdr_stats.py` charset tables). RFC2047 encoded-words are only in ~4% of members (`=?…?B?…?` in 38/900 spam and 31/900 ham subject lines, `research/enc_domains.py`).

Header names must be read as structured fields, not substring-matched.

- Balanced accuracy is the mean of per-class recall (≈ mean of TPR and TNR), so nothing but class-wise recall matters; pick the decision threshold on out-of-fold scores rather than the default 0.5 (`scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html`, `scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/classification_threshold.html`).
- Threshold calibration alone tends to move balanced accuracy more than class weights alone; if you add weighting, verify both recalls on held-out folds (`arxiv.org/html/2409.19751v1`).
- Stratified K-fold over the 3.6k labeled pages, with a duplicate/near-duplicate check between train and the folded-out set — spammer templates recur, so a leaked template pair inflates scores and hurts the hidden `.x` split (corpus inspection; slide 4 tip "develop a proper and flexible evaluation setup", `resources/smartlab-spam.txt`).
- Two-stage feature pipeline (text view + numeric structural view) joined before the classifier — HTML pages differ wildly in size, so keep the numeric block independent of vocabulary drift.
- Use a lenient HTML parser and guard against truncated/malformed documents and non-UTF-8 bytes (the corpus declares `iso-8859-1`), otherwise per-file crashes silently drop features or whole pages (`data/data/webspam-train/*` headers).
- If a page fails to parse or has no visible text, emit a sentinel vector instead of skipping it, so train/test feature counts stay aligned.

- Character/word n-gram bag over *normalized* source, TF-IDF-weighted, cosine similarity: works because these are text scripts, and n-grams survive identifier renaming. Character n-grams + cosine are the reported winner in style/authorship clustering on similar small text corpora (https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-1609/16090984.pdf); byte/char n-gram cosine is also the backbone of a whole-text classifier (http://www.cs.cmu.edu/~ralf/papers/brown-tsd13.pdf).
- Two-stage read-then-normalize: strip whitespace/comments, lowercase, collapse literals (`"..."`→STR, digits→NUM, `$var`→VAR) so variant families of the same shell line up; then n-grams on both raw and normalized text and concatenate views. Justification: webshells in this corpus are heavily obfuscated wrappers, so raw-text distance alone misses the payload (https://scantitan.com/malware-code-analyzer — "encoded eval", "layered decode chain", "character building"; https://github.com/bediger4000/php-malware-analysis/blob/master/webshells/wso_in_depth/README.md — same shell family evolves across versions, so only conserved features are stable).
- De-obfuscation expansion as a *feature source*, not just preprocessing: iterative base64/gzinflate/gzuncompress/str_rot13/hex decoding of string literals and hashing the decoded layer's n-grams. Real PHP webshells from 2010–2012 honeypot captures are `eval(gzinflate(base64_decode(...)))` chains several layers deep (https://scantitan.com/malware-code-analyzer, https://github.com/bediger4000/php-malware-analysis/blob/master/webshells/wso_in_depth/README.md).
- Behavioural/vocabulary vector from static string and call mining: which dangerous PHP functions appear (`eval`, `base64_decode`, `str_rot13`, `preg_replace`, `file_put_contents`, `curl_*`, `system`/`exec`/`passthru`), C&C command set (file manager, SQL console, self-delete, bind/back-connect), POST parameter names, and language markers (Russian-language shells are a known lineage signal) (https://huntress.com/threat-library/malware/php-webshell, https://github.com/bediger4000/php-malware-analysis/blob/master/webshells/wso_in_depth/README.md). These are the features that transfer to *unseen* families, unlike surface text.
- Cheap structural signal worth adding: line/byte length, `<?php` vs raw Perl shebang, ratio of comment/HTML text to code, presence of one giant encoded blob, count of distinct functions defined. Task says the corpus mixes PHP and Perl (task.md), so a language/capability flag should gate other features.

- Char/token n-gram vectors with **TF-IDF normalization + cosine distance**. The malware-clustering survey states that for high-dimensional sparse static features (strings, n-grams) the decisive factor is cosine/spherical geometry or TF-IDF normalization before Euclidean, which removes file-length effects — relevant here because honeypot webshells vary widely in size (`https://arxiv.org/html/2611.02380v1`).

The large web-shell study used code fingerprints for feature enumeration and found the shells are comparatively simple PHP (no OOP, minimal inter-procedural analysis), so a flat function/string-level fingerprint is tractable (`https://www.securitee.org/files/webshells_www2016.pdf`).

The WWW2016 analysis documents that families evolve by obfuscation and code copying (e.g. c99 → c999, c99 code inside Fx29), and ESDA-style work puts regex/deobfuscation before feature extraction (`https://www.securitee.org/files/webshells_www2016.pdf`, `https://actsoft.org/science/act2025-pro/60-esda2025.pdf`).
